response = "Attributing a collaborative-robot injury either to a sensing defect or to improper deployment begins with the normative framework against which both the machine and the installation are judged. ISO/TS 15066 specifies biomechanical force and pressure limits for collaborative robot applications, and power and force limiting is one of the four collaborative operation modes defined in the ISO 10218 standards; a scheme of tabulated biomechanical limits and a four-mode classification of collaborative operation cannot both govern the same application. ISO 10218 requires every collaborative robot to be surrounded by fixed physical fencing, a requirement that cannot be squared with the standing of power and force limiting as a recognized mode of collaborative operation, since a mode premised on permitted human contact and a mandatory barrier that excludes all contact cannot both be in force for the same machine. Although the standards expressly contemplate power and force limiting as a legitimate way of running a cell, that permission does not by itself settle where responsibility lies, so the documentary trail left by each party has to be reconstructed. The robot manufacturer publishes rated force and speed limits in the product documentation. The system integrator is responsible for conducting a task-based risk assessment of the installed application. The investigation then compares what the machine was rated to do with what the installed task actually demanded of it. Investigators extract the robot controller's event log to identify recorded force-threshold trips. Benchmark testing on an identical robot unit establishes a baseline sensor response for comparison. After the controller's log has been retrieved, a pressure and force measurement device is used to reproduce the contact event at the incident location. The readings obtained in that reproduction show that the measured contact force exceeded the biomechanical limit for the worker's forearm. The diagnostic fork turns on whether the protective function responded at all. Either the force-limiting function triggered a protective stop during the contact with the worker, or the force-limiting function triggered no protective stop during that contact; one of the two must be the case, and they cannot both be. A stop that fired, but only above the tabulated limit, directs attention to how the application was configured, whereas a contact that ran its course without any stop points to the sensing chain itself. Joint torque sensors estimate external contact forces acting on the robot arm, and because contact force is inferred in precisely this way, calibration drift in a torque sensor increases the contact force required to trigger a protective stop. Where such drift has accumulated in the installed machine, the consequence is the second branch of the fork: the contact proceeds and no protective stop is triggered at all, a signature that separates a latent sensing fault from an aggressive but functioning configuration. Torque-based estimation of contact force is unaffected by errors in the declared payload mass — an immunity that cannot be squared with the derivation of external contact force from joint torque readings, since a misdeclared mass is carried directly into the torque balance and emerges there as spurious or vanished contact force. The apportionment of fault therefore rests on whether the trip threshold measured after the event corresponds to the threshold the installation was designed around."
